book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter

chapters.relation: Breikss reads the Hannibal-Will bond as Sedgwick-style homosociality filtered through gift theory: Mauss and Bataille explain how Hannibal's lavish dinner parties and mentorship function as gifts that assert dominance, overwhelming Will until his inner voice becomes Hannibal's. Girard's mimetic desire then maps the rivalry's escalation — Alana as the shared object, Will's proxy murder attempt via Matthew Brown, the killing of Randall Tier that merges the two men into the 'Willdigo', and Mason Verger as the scapegoat whose death would have purged the conflict. Foucault's reading of Bosch's 'Cutting the Stone' casts Will as the patient and Hannibal as the doctor 'far more insane than the patient', with Jack and Alana as unwitting accomplices in the psychiatric stripping of Will's life, while Bataille's Erotism frames the cannibal feasts as transgression that heightens rather than abolishes the taboo.

chapters.file: ch24 - 12. A Little Empathy for Hannibal Is a Dangerous Thing.md
chapters.relation: Jones argues that Hannibal turns the therapy-room virtue of empathy into a horror: Will's profiling works by inhabiting a killer's frame of reference in Carl Rogers' sense, but empathic contact with Hannibal is framed so seductively — the fungi victim of 'Amuse-Bouche', the 'Sorbet' dinner party where the camera makes the viewer share his smirk — that Will, and before him Dr. Du Maurier, cannot pull their own moral perspective back out. The chapter ends by staging a fantasy Rogerian session in which a fearless therapist uncovers Hannibal's contempt for the weak as self-hatred for the powerless boy of Hannibal Rising, yet concludes that until such therapy is really possible, Rifkin's 'global peak empathy' world is one best walked away from.

chapters.file: ch25 - V. It’s Beautiful in Its Own Way, Giving Voice to the Unmentionable.md

chapters.relation: Holt argues that the key to Lecter is aestheticism: the Goldberg Variations scoring his nightstick killing of the Memphis guard is no camouflage, because art, cannibalism, murder and etiquette are all unified by aesthetic value prized apart from the good and the true. His 'ACME question' applies inference to the best explanation to show that a single hypothesis — the aesthetic — explains Art, Cannibalism, Murder and Etiquette together, with 'Discourtesy is unspeakably ugly to me' read as an aesthetic rather than a moral complaint. The final twist is that Lecter's psychopathic 'moral blindness' may enhance his powers of aesthetic discrimination the way literal blindness enhances hearing and touch.

chapters.file: ch27 - 14. A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Dinner Party.md
chapters.relation: Westfall sorts Lecter's humor into mockery ('I hope you're not too ugly'), expressions of power ('Are you setting a new standard of care?', delivered while hanging from a noose), and inside jokes ('I'm having an old friend for dinner', 'I wouldn't do that to the food, Tobias'), arguing against Noël Carroll that something can be frightening and funny at once because the joke is itself an exercise of power. He shows how the television series converts Harris's cruel mockery into displays of control, and how in-jokes addressed to the audience — Mikkelsen's census-taker callback to Hopkins's fava-beans line — pull viewers into complicity, a subtle fourth-wall break that is itself an expression of power.

Zanin takes FBI profiler John Douglas's maxim 'if you want to understand the artist, you have to look at the painting' and argues, with Croce's expression theory, Novitz's everyday aesthetics and Hegel's account of art and freedom, that Lecter's murders genuinely are artworks: Paul the butcher's head arranged in a suiban vessel with a 'Momund, Boucherie de Qualite' tag, Dortlich's head on the tree stump that recalls the charcoal stump in Lecter's cell drawing, and Rinaldo Pazzi's disemboweling staged like a Deposition painting over Florence. Against Hegel's restriction of art to pleasing beauty, the chapter claims revulsion is as much an aesthetic response as glorification, so that murder can be Aristotle's techne — the skill by which Lecter lives.

chapters.file: ch29 - VI. The Beauty and Art and Horror of Everything This World Has to Offer.md

chapters.relation: Shaw explains our identification with Lecter through mirror neurons triggered by Demme's extreme close-ups, Lecter's impeccable aesthetic and culinary taste, his evil-genius plotting, and his choice of 'free range rude' victims — but the deepest ground is Nietzsche's will to power, quoting The Gay Science and The Antichrist on the feeling of power as what makes action valuable. Lecter is read as Nietzsche's Overman in complete control of himself, his environment, and his inferiors, and the TV series confirms the theory because, with the black humor and romance stripped away, Mikkelsen's Lecter out-plots Will, Jack and Alana alike and walks triumphant from the Season 2 finale, having played everyone 'like his beloved Theremin'.

chapters.file: ch31 - 17. The Beguiling Horror of Hannibal Lecter.md
chapters.relation: Devlin and Biderman apply Noël Carroll's account of the monster and the paradox of horror to Lecter: as with Dracula, Freddy and Jason, audiences are horrified by and yet attracted to him, paying the price of fear and disgust for the pleasure of learning about the creature. But Lecter breaks Carroll's definition because he is a scientifically possible human being — his menace comes from intelligence, charm, persuasion and heightened senses rather than supernatural impossibility — so the authors widen the definition with Cynthia Freeland's realist monster, a creature embodying moral and social perversion. His rich mythos, from Mischa's death in Hannibal Rising to his tenderness toward Starling, makes him a tragic human monster whose back-story deepens both repulsion and attraction.

McClelland argues Lecter is a flawed healer: reading Starling's FBI disgrace as social exclusion, he shows how Lecter's hypnotic drugs and deep-hypnosis 'treatment' let her revisit and metabolize her repressed rage at her dead father — the parental imago he named back in Silence of the Lambs — producing a chrysalis-like metamorphosis completed when she defies Krendler at the dinner and asks for more of his brains. The healing is symmetric, since Starling's insight into Lecter's own Mischa fixation releases him too, and the chapter closes with an Aristotelian verdict — choice reveals character, and whether the couple's Buenos Aires partnership counts as good depends on long-term flourishing we have not yet seen.

holes.name: René Girard
holes.what: French theorist of mimetic desire: we borrow our desires from models who become rivals, and the resulting reciprocal violence is resolved by scapegoating a victim.
holes.why: Chapter 23 structures its entire account of the Hannibal-Will rivalry (Alana as shared object, the Randall Tier killing, Mason Verger as scapegoat) on Girard's mimetic desire, mimetic violence and scapegoat mechanism.

holes.name: Mimetic Desire and the Scapegoat Mechanism
holes.what: Desire imitated from a model who then becomes a rival, escalating into mimetic violence that ends when a scapegoat absorbs the community's conflict.
holes.why: Chapter 23 applies this sequence step by step to Will, Hannibal and Alana, and to Mason Verger's sacrificial death.

holes.name: Georges Bataille
holes.what: French philosopher of the 'accursed share' (the Necessary expenditure of surplus) and of transgression: taboos exist to be violated in ritual ways without being destroyed.
holes.why: Chapter 23 reads Hannibal's feasts as Bataille's display of social surplus and his cannibalism as transgression that heightens rather than abolishes the taboo on killing and corpse-violation.

holes.name: Homosociality
holes.what: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's term for the non-sexual bonds of friendship, mentorship and rivalry between men that organize desire and power.
holes.why: Chapter 23's thesis is that Hannibal's 'rare gift' to Will is precisely such a homosocial bond, developed explicitly through Sedgwick's Between Men.

holes.name: Empathy (Rogers' person-centered account)
holes.what: Carl Rogers' capacity to assume and communicate another person's internal frame of reference entirely without judgment, the foundation of client-centered therapy.
holes.why: Chapter 24 defines empathy through Rogers and argues that empathic contact with Hannibal destroys the empathizer's own moral perspective, as with Will and Dr. Du Maurier.

holes.name: Aestheticism (art for art's sake)
holes.what: The stance that aesthetic value is sovereign: art and beauty are to be pursued for their own sake, independent of moral or intellectual value.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues Lecter is an aesthete par excellence who ranks the beautiful above the good, and that his art, cannibalism, murder and etiquette all flow from that ranking.

holes.name: Noël Carroll
holes.what: Contemporary philosopher of art whose work on horror, humor and their shared incongruity structure is the reference point for philosophical discussion of the horror genre.
holes.why: Chapter 27 engages Carroll's claim that horror and humor are opposite mental states in order to argue that Lecter is funny and terrifying at the same time.

holes.name: The Incongruity Theory of Humor
holes.what: The view that we find funny what unites incongruous, incommensurable elements into a self-contradictory whole, as in the monster, the clown or the joke.
holes.why: Chapter 27 adopts incongruity theory as its first principle and applies it to Lecter's cannibal in-jokes such as 'I wouldn't do that to the food'.

holes.name: Benedetto Croce
holes.what: Italian idealist whose expression theory of art replaces beauty with expression, admitting the ugly and terrible into the aesthetic.
holes.why: Chapter 28 uses Croce's expression-centered aesthetics, and his idea of reality as 'the aesthetic oneness of opposites', to classify Lecter's murder tableaux as art.

holes.name: David Novitz
holes.what: Philosopher of art who tied art to everyday life, holding that debates over art track society's changing values and that the arts are the skills by which we live.
holes.why: Chapter 28 needs Novitz to move beyond art-as-skill (Aristotle's techne) to the claim that murder is the skill by which Hannibal Lecter lives.

holes.name: Noël Carroll
holes.what: Author of The Philosophy of Horror: the genre aims at fear and disgust directed at a threatening monster beyond current science, and our simultaneous attraction is the paradox of horror.
holes.why: Chapter 31 tests Lecter against Carroll's monster definition and paradox of horror, then argues he breaks both because he is a human, scientifically possible monster.

holes.name: Cynthia Freeland
holes.what: Philosopher of horror whose realist account defines the monster as any creature, however scientifically possible, that embodies social or moral perversion.
holes.why: Chapter 31 adopts Freeland's definition to explain why the human Lecter still counts as a monster and why his mythos deepens the paradox of horror.
